strengths: Well-motivated combination of GP kernel composition and SCM, with clear design justifications for the classification task
Comprehensive experimental evaluation addressing three well-defined research questions with extensive scaling law analysis (data, model, and training time)
Novel empirical finding that synthetic CAUKER data exhibits clean scaling laws while real-world UCR/UEA data shows irregular scaling, with mechanistic insights via non-linearity and CKA analysis
Strong practical results demonstrating sample efficiency: matching performance of larger real-trained models with ~20× fewer samples (Mantis) or ~1.3× (MOMENT)
Excellent reproducibility with detailed pseudocode, architectural specifications, and comprehensive hyperparameter documentation
Clear presentation and logical organization with effective visualizations and well-articulated design choices
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual components (GP kernels, SCM) from prior work; main contribution is combination which is incremental
Narrow experimental scope: only 2 foundation models tested, univariate-only, classification-only despite claims of broader applicability, no evaluation on domain-specific benchmarks beyond UCR
Insufficient justification of design choices: no ablation studies on critical decisions (activation functions, DAG structure, bank sizes), making it unclear which components are essential

Incomplete analysis of synthetic data quality: limited validation beyond DTW clustering and embeddings; missing comparison of statistical properties (autocorrelation, frequency characteristics); no validation that causal structure matters

Theoretical understanding gaps: why synthetic data exhibits clean scaling laws remains unexplained beyond superficial arguments; explanation for differences from forecasting scaling laws is underdeveloped
Evaluation protocol concerns: train-test overlap with UCR (acknowledged but problematic), unfair comparison with original models whose 'upper bounds' include UCR training data
Missing practical details: no computational cost analysis of generation, unclear when synthetic-only pretraining should be preferred over hybrid approaches, no discussion of failure modes
Risk of overfitting to UCR-specific characteristics: synthetic data exhibits artificial clean clustering not necessarily present in real classification tasks, limiting generalization

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models, pretraining paradigms, and 128 UCR datasets with systematic scaling law analysis
Well-motivated design combining kernel composition for temporal patterns with SCM for dependencies; design choices validated through ablations
Interesting empirical finding that synthetic CAUKER data exhibits clear scaling laws while real-world UEA data shows irregular behavior
Strong qualitative analysis including DTW clustering visualization, UMAP embeddings, non-linearity/CKA similarity metrics demonstrating learned representations
Extensive supplementary material with pseudocode, detailed experimental setup, and hyperparameter specifications supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: straightforward combination of existing GP kernel composition (Ansari et al. 2024) and SCM generation (Hollmann et al. 2023) with only mean function adaptation, representing primarily engineering contribution rather than fundamental methodological advance

Modest empirical improvements over appropriate baseline (Mean+KernelSynth): only 0.11% for Mantis and 1.68% for MOMENT (Table 1), with no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals despite margins within potential noise

Problematic OOD evaluation protocol: explicitly allows UCR train sets in pretraining while testing on UCR test sets, violating true out-of-distribution evaluation and enabling train/test overlap at dataset level; claims of OOD superiority are thus unsubstantiated

Unfair performance comparisons: original Mantis (78.66%) and MOMENT (78.85%) were trained on 1.89M and 13M series respectively including in-distribution UCR data, while claiming 'state-of-the-art' for synthetic-only pretraining achieving 78.55% and 77.49%; absolute performance does not exceed real-data-pretrained models

Scaling law claims overstated: attributing UEA's irregular scaling to inherent properties of real data rather than domain mismatch and limited diversity; forecasting literature (Yao et al. 2025) shows real data can exhibit clear scaling laws, undermining Finding #2

Severely limited experimental scope: only two TSFM models tested, only one benchmark (UCR), only univariate sequences of fixed length 512; recent architectures like UniTS omitted; generalization to multivariate/variable-length sequences not explored
Misleading 'causal' framing: SCM generates random DAG without true causal relationships; method captures structural dependencies, not causality; marketing language oversells actual contributions
Missing statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests despite small marginal improvements; no ablation on activation function bank design; sensitivity analysis absent

Hyperparameter design transparency issues: choice of 36 kernels appears arbitrary and may be empirically tuned on target task (UCR), raising concerns about task-specific overfitting in generator design

Reproducibility gaps: code availability not mentioned, exact sampling procedures for K, M, E, V underspecified, sensitivity to random DAG generation not explored, saturation effects (Figs 3-4) glossed over despite practical implications

strengths: Novel technical approach that cleverly combines GP kernel composition with SCM structure, addressing limitations of prior forecasting and tabular synthetic generators
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 128 UCR datasets with two different model architectures and pretraining paradigms
First systematic study of scaling laws for zero-shot time series classification, with mechanistic insights via non-linearity and CKA metrics
Strong sample efficiency results: achieving near-original model performance with 20× fewer samples (Mantis) and 1.3× fewer samples (MOMENT)
Well-motivated design choices with clear explanations for why CAUKER differs from prior work (inclusion of mean functions, causal structure)
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and comprehensive appendices supporting reproducibility
Practical significance: demonstrates that synthetic-only pretraining is viable for classification, distinguishing this from forecasting
weaknesses: Limited model scope: only two models tested (Mantis 8M, MOMENT 77M); unclear if findings generalize to other architectures, scales, or inductive biases
Evaluation restricted to classification only: transfer to forecasting, anomaly detection, or other tasks is untested, limiting practical applicability of TSFM pretraining

Insufficient explanation of scaling law phenomena: why do real-world datasets lack clean scaling? Why does synthetic structure enable scaling? Non-linearity/CKA analyses are correlational, not mechanistic
Unfair comparison with original models: original Mantis/MOMENT used UCR train sets (in-distribution) while CAUKER avoids them (OOD), making direct performance comparison problematic

Incomplete analysis of synthetic data: quantitative diversity metrics missing; no statistical characterization (ACF, frequency content, trend/seasonality properties); visual examples of generated vs. real series absent

Unexplained irregularities: MOMENT at 10M CAUKER shows non-monotonic scaling; saturation behavior at high model capacity not systematically explored; claims of 'clear and consistent scaling laws' overstated given these issues

Limited ablation studies: relative importance of kernel diversity vs. mean functions vs. SCM structure not disentangled; design choices (36 kernels, specific activation functions) appear ad-hoc without sensitivity analysis
Computational cost analysis missing: time to generate 10M series and comparison to real data collection/preprocessing costs not discussed, important for practical adoption

Overclaiming in presentation: title/abstract suggest SOTA performance, but results are comparable to existing methods with marginal differences; ~1% gap vs. real data not fully acknowledged in main claims
Loose causal framing: directed dependencies are not true causal relationships; terminology could be more precise

strengths: Novel and well-motivated approach combining GP kernel composition with SCMs, clearly bridging temporal structure and class separability—a thoughtful design that differentiates from prior forecasting/tabular generators

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 128 UCR datasets, WOODS benchmark, irregular clinical data, and extensions to forecasting; includes multiple model architectures (Mantis, MOMENT) with different pre-training paradigms

Significant practical finding: CAUKER enables ~20× sample efficiency (100K vs. 1.89M samples) with <0.1% accuracy drop for Mantis, and achieves competitive/superior OOD generalization across diverse domains

Discovery of clear monotonic scaling laws in synthetic data (10K-10M samples, 1M-783M parameters) contrasting with irregular scaling in real-world datasets—valuable insight challenging assumptions about large-scale pre-training necessity

Thorough ablations and qualitative analyses (DTW clustering, attention rollout, CKA similarity, UMAP projections) strengthen claims; hyperparameter sensitivity study (Tables 4-5) demonstrates robustness
Excellent reproducibility: promised code release, detailed pseudocode, 30-page appendix with implementation details, and systematic experimental protocols
Extensions beyond main task (forecasting with Chronos, irregular multivariate data) demonstrate broader applicability without task-specific modifications
weaknesses: Limited model coverage: only 2 architectures (Mantis 8M, MOMENT 77M) evaluated; many recent TSFMs (NuTime, UniTS, TIMER, state-space models, LLM-based approaches) untested, limiting generalizability claims despite acknowledged computational constraints

Univariate-only evaluation is a core limitation not adequately addressed; multivariate capability relegated to future work; treating channels independently discards important inter-channel dependencies; the circular justification ('match univariate pre-training regime') is insufficient

In-distribution advantage of baseline models (original Mantis/MOMENT saw UCR train splits) creates unfair comparison; while acknowledged in Table 7, main claims emphasize OOD evaluation, which may not reflect practitioner priorities; Spectro domain degradation (-5.5%) highlights this issue

Statistical rigor concerns: no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests across 128 UCR results; marginal improvements (78.31 vs. 78.20) lack statistical validation; standard deviations reported only for auxiliary metrics

Incomplete justification of design choices: why this kernel-SCM combination is optimal unclear; limited ablation on alternatives; random DAG structure doesn't represent true causality (terminology 'causal' oversells contribution); Table 1 shows SCM alone underperforms but lacks deeper analysis of its contribution

Scaling laws claims need stronger evidence: only 2 models shown; unclear if UEA's 'irregular' scaling is inherent or due to poor curation; better-curated real data might exhibit similar scaling (not investigated); causality direction unclear

Limited characterization of synthetic data properties: beyond clustering visualizations (Figure 2) and SWD comparison (Table 6), deeper analysis of class separability, entropy, or what makes CAUKER suitable for classification is missing; minimal investigation of how kernel/activation/mean function choices affect performance

Forecasting extension (Section J) feels incomplete: only Chronos tested; results 2-3% behind official models despite 160× fewer observations; unclear if CAUKER is classification-optimized and how general findings are across tasks

Hyperparameter adaptation guidance lacking: no systematic study of which time series characteristics CAUKER handles poorly; Tables 4-5 show robustness in narrow range; no domain-specific adaptation strategy; failure modes (e.g., Spectro) inadequately analyzed

Multivariate extension promised but not delivered; current approach on irregular multivariate data (Table 13) shows mixed/competitive results with less analysis; significantly limits real-world applicability where multivariate data dominates

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (Mantis, MOMENT) and benchmarks (UCR, WOODS, clinical datasets)
Well-motivated approach combining GP kernel composition with SCM to generate causally coherent synthetic time series with temporal structure
Extensive supplementary material (30-page appendix) with ablations, qualitative analyses, and reproducibility details
Addresses a practical problem: enabling synthetic data pre-training for time series classification TSFMs
Clear presentation of method with pseudocode and implementation details; code release promised
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparison: Original Mantis/MOMENT were pre-trained on corpora including UCR train splits (in-distribution), while CAUKER is purely out-of-distribution. Claims of matching/exceeding performance are misleading under these different evaluation protocols.

Overstated 'scaling laws' finding: The clean scaling of CAUKER vs. irregular scaling of UEA is confounded by domain mismatch (UEA→UCR transfer) and heterogeneity in real data. The paper doesn't investigate whether curated real data would show better scaling. This is an artifact of data curation, not a fundamental discovery.

Limited technical novelty: CAUKER primarily combines existing components (GP kernel composition from Ansari et al. 2024; SCM from Hollmann et al. 2023). Adding non-zero mean functions to GP is standard practice. The core contribution is incremental.

Marginal improvements over simpler baselines: Table 1 shows CAUKER only marginally outperforms Mean+KernelSynth (0.11% for Mantis, 1.68% for MOMENT). The contribution of the SCM layer is insufficiently justified; unclear whether improvements come from causal structure, added nonlinearity, or other factors.

Shallow analysis of mechanisms: Section 4.1 qualitative analysis (Figure 2 clustering) is suggestive but doesn't rigorously establish why causal structure is necessary. Ablations (Tables 4-5) demonstrate robustness but not sensitivity. Why synthetic data enables scaling laws remains unexplained.

Limited scope and generalization: Evaluation restricted to two encoder-based models; no evaluation on decoder-only architectures, older models, or other recent TSFMs. Univariate-only; multivariate deferred to future work. Forecasting relegated to appendix despite method's claimed generality.

Unexplained performance instabilities: MOMENT-783M on CAUKER-10M degrades vs. CAUKER-1M (Table 8). Fine-tuning results (Table 12) show CAUKER-100K underperforms significantly (82.91% vs. 84.96%), requiring 10× more data to approach parity. These suggest overfitting or optimization issues not adequately addressed.

Experimental design issues: Inconsistent dataset sizes for Mantis (100K) vs. MOMENT (10M) complicate scaling law comparison; no ablation justifying these choices. No statistical significance testing; confidence intervals absent despite small accuracy differences (e.g., 0.11%). Stability across random seeds not discussed.
Missing depth in comparisons: No comparison to simpler baselines (ARIMA, VAE-based synthetic data). No semi-synthetic approaches. Power-law exponents for scaling laws not formally reported.

Domain-wise performance degradation: CAUKER-100K underperforms on Spectro domain (-5.5%, Table 9). While explanation provided (small datasets favor ID baseline), this limitation reveals the method's non-universal applicability and should be more prominently discussed.

strengths: Well-motivated synthesis combining GP kernel composition with SCM, clearly articulating why neither component alone suffices for time series classification
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 128 UCR datasets, 17 WOODS datasets, with systematic data and model scaling studies (10K-10M samples, 1M-783M parameters)
Novel finding that CAUKER exhibits clear monotonic scaling laws while real-world benchmarks show irregular scaling—valuable insight into what makes training data suitable for TSFMs
Strong practical impact: achieves competitive performance with ~20× fewer pre-training samples (Mantis: <0.1% drop) and ~1.3× fewer for MOMENT (1% drop)
Extensive reproducibility efforts including public code, detailed pseudocode, comprehensive ablations, and multiple supplementary analyses (attention rollout, clustering, embedding visualizations)
Demonstrates transferability across different pre-training paradigms (contrastive and masked reconstruction), architectures (ViT and Transformer), and tasks (classification and forecasting)
weaknesses: Limited theoretical justification for why the GP+SCM combination generates class-discriminative training data; the synthesis appears somewhat ad-hoc without principled analysis of emergent properties

Fairness concerns in main comparisons: original Mantis and MOMENT were pre-trained on corpora including UCR train splits while CAUKER is strictly OOD, making direct comparison less clean and complicating claims of superiority
Evaluation limited to two TSFM architectures and primarily classification task; while Chronos forecasting extension exists, main contributions focus narrowly on classification

Insufficient analysis of what specific CAUKER properties drive performance—clustering analysis (Figure 2) is brief; missing systematic ablation comparing class structure, temporal patterns, and causal dependencies separately
Most results lack error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, making it unclear if small differences (0.1-0.5%) are meaningful or noise
Hyperparameter choices (kernel families, activation functions, composition ranges) lack principled justification; ablations show robustness but not design rationale

Multivariate extension limited to treating channels separately; paper misses potential benefits of capturing cross-variable dependencies (acknowledged as future work but significantly limits applicability)
Missing computational analysis: no comparison of wall-clock pre-training time for 10M synthetic vs. 1.89M real samples, making sample efficiency claims incomplete
All experiments fixed at sequence length 512; sensitivity to different lengths and interaction with model-specific design choices unexplored
Failure mode analysis sparse: Spectro domain degradation (-5.5%) hand-waved as small-sample artifact without systematic investigation of when CAUKER struggles
